That gives us bilibili the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days shows how quickly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻

What I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly important... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️

Most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨

InfoQ Homepage News TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class

Nov 06, 2026 3 min read

Microsoft has released TypeScript 7.1 Beta, the first update to the Go-based native compiler that landed as TypeScript 7.0 in July, and the release that finally hands tool authors a programmatic API again. Daniel Rosenwasser announced the beta on 20 October 2026, and the team pointed developers to it on X, inviting feedback ahead of a release candidate and stable build that the iteration plan tentatively places in late November, though the beta itself arrived two weeks behind schedule.

The headline change restores the compiler API that 7.0 dropped. For three months anything that embedded the compiler, from Vue’s Volar to Svelte, Astro, ts-morph and type-aware linting, was stranded on TypeScript 6. Rather than revive the old monolithic module, 7.1 splits it into focused entry points such as typescript/sync, typescript/async, typescript/fs and typescript/ast, paths that previously sat behind an unstable prefix now dropped to signal intent. The client also models incremental edits through reusable snapshots, so an editor can derive new state from an old one without rebuilding the world, and the team says the surface will stay backward compatible across all of 7.x once stable.

Sitting on top of that is the beta’s most discussed feature, content mappers, a supported plugin point that lets a package hand TypeScript a virtual view of a non-standard file such as a .vue or .svelte component, with mappings back to the original so errors point at the right line. Because a mapper runs as a separate process it executes only when you opt in, and the team warns the flag should be treated like any build plugin.

Vue’s language tools are already porting to it: maintainer Johnson Chu has shipped Vue Language Tools v4 alpha on top of content mappers, dropping the separate vue-tsc binary in favour of a @vue/content-mapper that runs inside tsc itself. In a hands-on migration write-up, the Directus admin app, 581 Vue components across 882 TypeScript files saw type checks fall from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds on tsc 7.1 plus the mapper, a 4.6x speedup over vue-tsc 3. The author also flagged that teams adopting the beta would need to run 7.1 in CI alongside an older TypeScript in the editor until Vue tooling stabilises on top of the stable release.

Microsoft’s MUI docs benchmark falls from 22.2 to 11.9 seconds while roughly halving memory, though heavier codebases such as VS Code see closer to 1.2x. An independent test against NestJS put a 353,000 line check at 2.76 seconds on the beta against 4.95 on 7.0 and 12.42 on the old compiler, while flagging a 7.0 memory regression that 7.1 reverses.

On GitHub, Akira Higuchi reported that, in a particular editor workflow, saving a mapper’s watched configuration file could leave types stale until the language server is restarted. The issue remains open.

The language itself gains import attributes in ambient module declarations, TC39 source phase imports for loading WebAssembly, and a stable es2026 target carrying additions like Math.sumPrecise() and Error.isError().

Teams still on TypeScript 5 should move through 6 to 7, and projects using Vue, Svelte or Angular should keep a dual TypeScript 6 and 7 install until their framework tooling ships a 7.1 build. Tool and library authors are urged to port to the new entry points now and to flag missing functions through the API status tracker while gaps can still be filled before stable. The independent numbers are a reminder that the native compiler now sets the bar, with rival type checkers on Hacker News already measuring themselves against tsgo 7.1 beta.

TypeScript is an open-source programming language developed and maintained by Microsoft. It builds on JavaScript by adding optional static typing, catching errors before code runs and making large codebases easier to build and maintain with confidence. Since version 7.0 its compiler has been written in Go rather than in TypeScript itself, a native port that underpins the speed gains in this release, and it remains widely adopted across the frontend and backend ecosystems, with first-class support in frameworks such as React, Angular, Vue and Node.js.

#9929. Datacenters, Elon Musk, and AI are all on the chopping block once Congress changes hands in 2027

Rage, rage against the dying of the right

Hey, did you hear about those elections in the US this past week?

The Democratic party has seized control of Congress and state governments around the country. It's easy to see this entirely as a rebuke of Trump and his policies, but blowback against AI, datacenters, and the tech industry played a role too, if the past week of chaos in markets and Silicon Valley is any indication.

Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg Editor In Chief Matt Rosoff, and special guest, senior reporter at The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto, to talk about what the winds of political change mean for the tech industry.

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and hey, chances are you've heard about those elections we had in the US this week. The Democratic Party dealt a pretty hearty rebuke to Donald Trump, Republicans, and the MAGA movement, with Dems winning elections in states that haven't gone blue in decades. Now it's easy to see this as a blowback against Trump and Republican politics. There's a lot of indication that the tech industry was kind of on the ballot this year, too.

After all, they cozied up hard to Trump in his first two years in office in a bid to push AI and promote datacenter projects, and people have been none too happy about any of that. With me to discuss the elections and what they mean for Silicon Valley is Reg editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and a special guest this week, senior reporter from The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto. Thank you both for coming on, and welcome, Liz.

I was so glad we could make this work. So let's start off by dissecting the degree to which AI datacenters and attitudes toward the tech industry in general sort of played a role in this election. I mean, were those major elements in the Democratic sweep or just part of the equation?

I think they were part of the equation. I think first and foremost people were pissed off about the corruption. And second, people were pissed off about ICE. Having people snatched from your community is the sort of thing that kind of sticks with you. So I think those were probably the two biggest issues. But the corruption is not totally separate from the tech industry, given the way that the tech industry has been cozying up with Donald Trump, the fact that Elon Musk and DOGE were cruising through the federal government, destroying stuff. So those things are related.

And then obviously there's the datacenter stuff, which is universally unpopular, not the only bipartisan issue in the US right now, but certainly a big one. So it's in there, I think.

I thought it was interesting that of something like 47 anti-datacenter initiatives on local ballots, 45 of them passed and only one failed. So that seems to me to be some indication that people at least don't like whatever these things are being shoved down their throats, which is funny because two years ago nobody knew what a datacenter was.

I think that there are sort of two things happening here, right? The first is that a lot of these datacenters have been popping up in people's communities without a robust public comment period. There have been a lot of NDAs being used and backroom deals. And I think most people don't like that stuff anyway. But add to that how frustrated I think a lot of people are with the tech industry right now. And suddenly this is the avatar of the tech industry doing a bunch of things that people don't like. And they can't get rid of Elon Musk. They can't pry Sundar Pichai out of his CEO role. There's not a lot you can really do, but you can stop the datacenter.

They can't get rid of AI results in search.

I think that's just an expression of that frustration, right?

Yeah, and I think the industry at least has to see it a little bit, right? Because I think it was maybe the day after the elections, OpenAI came out right away and was like, "Hey, you know what we're going to do? We're going to really try to be better civic citizens in our communities. We're going to stop signing NDAs." And then they're also trying to rebrand datacenters as "compute campuses" to make them more attractive, as these aren't just big warehouses where we're doing AI processing. We're trying to do all this other stuff there, too. It just seemed like there's very much an awareness that, "Oh wow, this may have been a bit of a blowback against us, or at the very least, something we're going to need to adapt to in a new political cycle."

I found it really interesting: I saw a study yesterday, maybe the day before, that said 41 percent of active datacenter projects are in states that Democrats took control of this election cycle, including Texas and my home state of Michigan, where Democrats didn't just capture federal offices, but state-level legislatures and offices as well. That could potentially mean that a lot of datacenter projects are going to be slowed or stalled completely in the next few years. Is there any indication that that could happen, you think?

Well, maybe. I think that the frustration with datacenters has really been growing over the last two years. And you've seen things like Project Jupiter in New Mexico where the locals didn't even know who was coming in, right? There was total secrecy. And then as soon as people figured out what was going on, they made the moves they could to start blocking access to power.

And so I think anybody who's politically ambitious picks up on that and says, "Okay, this is a way to really channel some populist frustration. I can probably ride this." So there's that part of it. But I also think these people got elected a couple days ago. And in some cases, I think this was a race in Iowa, the Democrat had dropped out because he was sick and got elected anyway. So there's a certain amount of just pure rage being expressed here.

I've heard a lot of people saying that it wasn't even necessarily a vote for Democrats in many cases as it was a vote against Republicans and their policies.

Yeah, so I think that using that as a way to consolidate power is a smart move, right? So you see even before election night's out, there are these statements like "lawyer up." And  I imagine investigating DOGE is going to be super popular because a lot of people lost their jobs, right? Separately from all of the people who died because USAID stopped. I think that there is just a real political will for investigations, for some of this stuff becoming public. And specifically in Texas, you have these emails between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott that have been really heavily redacted. You want a fast and easy political win, you unredact those emails.

And I can't imagine that the new governor of Texas isn't going to — leave it to the Democrats to take something like this and completely squander it by sitting on their thumbs and trying to compromise. So part of me is like, "Wow, what a mandate you have. Let's see how badly you mess this up." I'm hoping that isn't the case. I'm hoping that we see some actual drive from Democrats to do things like unredact those emails. Give voters a reason to actually say you did something good, right? It's easy, like we were talking a couple of minutes ago again about datacenters kind of being a scapegoat for the tech industry right now. And Elon Musk is easily that as well, right? He's the person you can point to and say, "Look at this asshole," and all the things he's been doing, especially in Texas, right?  I'm hoping that they do take that and run with it. He's been—

I think it's interesting. Texas didn't just elect a couple Democrats. It was a Democratic slate from top to bottom. And I think a lot of Trump voters showed up specifically to vote against Republicans this time. So I don't know if that's all—some of that is related to Paxton being on the ballot and the sort of known history of corruption that he's shown and the fact that the MAGA movement backed him so boldly. But some of it is, I think, Elon being so loud and so belligerent and charging in and saying we're just going to do whatever we want and get out of the way. And there has kind of been an arrogance among the tech industry and the tech executives for the past few years, but I think it's really become loud in the last couple of years. And I think to some degree, datacenters are a backlash against that and some of the ire directed towards Elon Musk is a backlash against that.

We all live in the same society, right? We've been hearing Sam Altman out here like, "Well, some people are going to die because of AI, and we're just going to have to accept that as a cost." And it's like, well, Sam, is that you? Are you planning to die for AI? Because it kind of sounds like you're talking about me and I don't like it.

Right. Yeah, it's the same sort of thing with wars. Some of you are going to have to die. Me and my kids, we're fine. Politicians are never going to send their sons and daughters to fight these wars.

I was recently in Washington and talking to some folks there who are involved with federal agencies and the difference between how Silicon Valley and tech companies and startups think of and use AI. I mean, it's $10,000 token budgets per developer and everybody's using agents to automate workflows and everything. And in Washington, it's like, this went way too far, way too fast. How do we stop it? And meanwhile, now AI is uncovering flaws and vulnerabilities in all of this software and all of these online services and web servers that we've been using for 25 years. So we've got to figure out how to patch all of that. We've got people entering confidential information into Chinese models like DeepSeek. So I think that the tech industry got way ahead of itself and the rest of the country is just starting to catch up. And yeah, maybe in five or ten years we will all be using agents and the infrastructure will have been built out to a point where the costs make sense and the ROI makes sense. But right now there's just this huge disconnect it seems between tech insiders in Silicon Valley and how people actually are using the technology today. So there may be some of that as well.

I think that there is a bubble, an intellectual bubble around Silicon Valley where all of these people are talking to each other and hanging out on X and assuring each other they're the smartest. And they're saying things like, "Oh, this is going to totally change your life." And the normal person who is using ChatGPT to try to replace their search engine is noticing that ChatGPT kind of hallucinates and it's not it's not that good. And there is this impulse on the part of these evangelists to be like, "Well, that's your problem because you don't know how to properly prompt the AI." And it's like, uh-uh, that's not how you get people to adopt technology. If you remember the internet, when the World Wide Web first happened, people didn't start using it until it made sense for them to use it. There were people who liked it because tech was their hobby and they thought it was a cool toy. But it wasn't until there was a reason for ordinary people to start using it that ordinary people started using it. Even online shopping, which I think is one of the very obvious use cases for the internet and was very early on, didn't catch up to in-person shopping for 20 years. So all of this hyperventilating around AI and how it's going to change the entire society and eliminate everybody's job and all of this other stuff, I feel like it's really misplaced. And it's not just misplaced because it underestimates the experience the rest of us are having with AI, which is frankly not that great. You're going to replace my job with this? Good luck.

Also there's just this sort of reality check. If you think about what AI is, it does certain kinds of intellectual work really well. Programming, for instance. Mathematics. But those are not things that require human relationships or resources outside of a computer. Almost all of the rest of us are involved in industries where those things are required. And so, how do you fit AI into that is a really different question. So there are blinders on in Silicon Valley and you can even see it — I live in Oakland and as soon as you leave San Francisco and go to Oakland, you start talking to normal people and they're just like, "I don't see the point of this AI. Why are we doing this?"

Yeah, I mean most people I talk to agree it's kind of useless to a degree, right? The way I think of it is it's almost like it's replaced Wikipedia for me, right? It's replaced — it hasn't even replaced search, it's replaced Wikipedia. It's the place I can go to get a basic overview of something to then do my own research because I can't trust the information that a Google search overview gives me, but at least it's going to maybe surface some resources that I didn't know were there, right?

It's good for summarizing certain kinds of documents. I do hear about it being used in the legal profession pretty extensively. So you don't have to read every line of every briefing. You have to check its work, because sometimes it makes stuff up or invents citations. I think it's gotten better at that.

You know, it's good for things like cleaning up text and it is good for programming. I hear a lot of programmers saying, "Hey, we were using this internal software or we were using a couple of our licenses of a particular enterprise piece of software to accomplish one very specific task and it was too expensive and we vibe coded a replacement for it over the weekend and it actually works. It's good enough. And we don't have to pay enterprise vendor X ten thousand dollars a month or something anymore."

Yeah, just make sure it's not exposed to the internet or next thing you know.

Right. It's not handling any sensitive data that you care about. Right, exactly.

Yeah, I mean I generally think of AI, at least in my experience, because I tend to not use it actually. I have moved to Kagi so that I can just get the old Google search circa 2012, primary source document type deal, because Google search sucks so much.

I think of it as being kind of a shitty intern, right? I occasionally use AI to transcribe my interviews and it's good enough. I have to double check it. I've got to listen to the part that I want to quote to make sure that it got it right, because sometimes it really doesn't. But it beats doing the transcription myself. So I have this kind of shitty intern now that I have to keep an eye on. And that's fine because that can be time saving if you need to change a format in an Excel spreadsheet. That feels like it's about the level at which the shitty intern does okay. But anything more serious than that, and I'm like, "I don't know about this. I think I'd better do it if it's going to be done right."

But is it worth $1,000 a month or $10,000 a month?

With the election and at the same time the finances of Anthropic becoming clearer and clearer and these increasing commitments. They filed their S-1 at precisely the right time when they had this growth spike and they were profitable for one quarter and then you looked at Q3 and lo and behold, they're back in the red again. I just wonder if some of this infrastructure buildout is going to be stalled and how that sort of affects pricing and how that affects competitiveness versus open weights models and those kinds of things. I don't know, I know Liz, you've looked at some of the financing in the industry, particularly around the CoreWeaves of the world, the neo-clouds, what do you think's going on there?

I think that those are only going to live as long as Nvidia wants them to live. You look at CoreWeave and it just doesn't make sense as a business. It's paying too much for debt to make sense as a business. There's just no way to get out from under that debt. And so, as long as Nvidia is willing to continue bailing them out, because it is basically an Nvidia client state – Nvidia is the reason that they were able to have an IPO at all. So as long as Nvidia is willing to bail them out, sure, they're going to continue being a going concern. But if you look at the bond market, people are pretty nervous about those bonds and I think they're right to be nervous. We saw here today – today is Friday – we saw Microsoft pulling out of a deal with Oracle for datacenter capacity for compute. The excuse that they gave was that Oracle had old chips. And maybe that is part of the decision-making, I don't know. I don't live in Microsoft. But it's also possible that Microsoft, who is building its own datacenters, is like, "Well, I don't need to give money to a competitor. We'll figure out something smarter to do in the meantime. And then once our datacenters are built, we'll just use our own."

And that has been the case for all of those neo-clouds for a while now, that their clients are about to become their competitors as the buildout happens. So if the buildout slows down, then every existing datacenter becomes more valuable. And so maybe that gives CoreWeave a lease on life. But maybe not, because who knows what's going to happen with the interest rates.

And how do you feel about Oracle? Their borrowing is getting more and more expensive and it seems like people are sort of walking away. Could Oracle actually be in some kind of real financial trouble?

I think that Oracle has enough going on in its legacy businesses that I doubt bankruptcy is on the table, but I could be wrong. I do think that they have made a really big bet on AI generally and OpenAI specifically, and I'm not sure that OpenAI was a super smart bet. Again, depending on how the buildout goes and what comes online and what doesn't, it might turn out that Oracle can turn around and flip that compute to somebody else if OpenAI isn't good for their money. It might also be the case that Oracle can use that compute itself for its other businesses. I am a little less worried about Oracle than I am about the pure play neo-clouds that basically pivoted from bitcoin mining and have no other business.

We've been talking about that almost weekly, because I feel like so often the Kettle ends up being about AI, right? Because that's the big topic right now. And almost every week we mention the fact that Oracle, Google, Microsoft, these companies are going to be fine if all this AI financing and circular investing starts to shrivel up, right? Who's not going to be fine is OpenAI and Anthropic. And the neo-clouds, right? They're all making these huge bets on AI and they have no other business to fall back on. It's not like someone's going to try to fall back on bitcoin at this point, I don't think.

Certainly not at this point. I mean, just looking at looking at what bitcoin did this week, I feel like it's not super valuable to be a bitcoin miner right now.

Let's talk about Elon Musk. Is this sort of the beginning of the bursting of the Musk worship bubble? Are we sort of seeing him lose his influence and power a little bit?

I know Liz wrote an article on all of the things he could have spent whatever it was, $500 million on.

Obviously he doesn't really know how to have a lot of fun, but the fact that he lost so completely everywhere that he bet, and the fact that Democrats are starting to whisper about indictments and investigations, is this sort of the end of his reign as the king of tech?

It's a good question. One of the things that's been interesting to me is that the Twitter acquisition really made the public turn on Elon Musk, right? That was when people were like, "Is he a genius? Because that doesn't seem like the move of a — why is he doing this?" And then of course, following that, the stuff with the Trump administration, people started protesting Tesla, like he kind of skunked his brand. So there is the popular view of Elon Musk, which is that this guy sucks. And then there is Silicon Valley, where for some reason he is still held in really high esteem. And I don't know why that is, except that maybe he's very good at raising money.

But that's real and that's still a thing. And so I am interested to see what happens here because if these sweetheart deals do start getting unearthed and we start seeing some of the private correspondence and like, "Oops, there might have been a little bit of bribery here and there," or "Oops, there might have been something else that was quasi-legal," those are things that are significant that become risks to his companies because they are so closely tied to him, right? For a long time, Tesla didn't have to buy advertising because Elon Musk's Twitter account was good enough. You know, and so you live with Elon Musk, you die with Elon Musk. That's just what it is. He can delete all the tweets he wants, but it doesn't change what we all saw over the last two years. And so I do think that there is a very real chance that he's got Texas where he's got an attorney general who entered basically with a mandate to investigate him. He has a senator who is like, "Hey, I'm proof that Texas can't be bought."

He's got a governor who isn't that fond of him either. And there's that. And then broadly across the country, again, this man is unpopular, so he's a great target for investigations.

I think we are looking at a real change of his fortunes. And whether that will stick or not is anybody's guess. Because one of the things that has certainly been true for the entire time that I have covered Elon Musk, which at this point is more than a decade, is that you discover which laws have teeth and which ones do not. Turns out copyright law really matters. Turns out the Chancery Court of Delaware counts. That one matters too.

I don't know about the SEC. I don't know that that's real.

Or like when he was smoking weed on camera and then got a slap on the wrist. I guess our drug laws around contractors, if you're rich enough, they don't matter. So there's a real sense in which we're going to find out exactly which laws apply to Elon Musk and which ones do not.

I also think it was interesting his purchase of Twitter and the way he sort of tilted the platform or the way the platform got tilted, so it kind of became this center-right, right-wing, Silicon Valley echo chamber. And I think a lot of people were surprised by the election results on Tuesday. As a result of that, if you're only on Twitter and talking to your very rich friends in VC, you might not actually know what real people think.

Yeah, there was a whole story I read about Bluesky basically saying, "Hey, we were right the whole time. Twitter's become this echo chamber of right-wing thought that doesn't realize that the rest of the world is a little pissed off at the tech industry." It's been kind of—

I think there isn't what Twitter used to be, which was where everyone was, right? After Musk bought Twitter, I think the social networks really fragmented. So I'm not going to sit here and — I like Bluesky, I use Bluesky. I don't think it's necessarily representative of the entire country. I think it is representative of a lot of people who are left-wing. And I think it can be useful in that way, in the same way that the left-wing blogosphere was useful in the early 2000s. That's a great way to organize, it's a great way to strategize. Fantastic. But similarly, I'm watching with a lot of schadenfreude the right-wing infighting on Twitter right now. They did not see this coming. And to be honest, neither did I. I knew there was going to be a blue wave; I did not think that my home state of Iowa was going to elect a bunch of Democrats. I didn't see Texas coming.

Yeah, no. I mean I figured [Texas Senator Elect James] Talarico was maybe a toss-up, right? But he beat [Republican Attorney General Ken] Paxton handily. You know, it was insane to see the degree to which people really blew back on Trump and, like we were saying, on the tech industry too, to a degree.

And if you think about the differences between Bluesky and X, there's another significant one, which is that X has an algorithm that is being tweaked by Elon Musk to show Elon Musk things he likes. And Bluesky, there are a bunch of algorithms that you can adopt, but I'm just using the same reverse chronology timeline that I have used forever on social media. And that again It's not going to show me just things I want to see. And so like again, like there are uses for algorithms, there are uses for filters, but you have to keep in mind that if you're being shown things you like, you're being shown things you like.

I think it's going to be interesting to see kind of what happens in the next — well, it's going to be at least a few months before things start happening, right? Because the new politicians who've been elected don't really take office until the beginning of the year. But once that happens, will the Democrats actually manage to do anything with this mandate they've been given? Will Elon Musk face some degree of accountability and will datacenter projects be stalled? Don't know.

Could happen, might not. Either way, we're gonna be here on the kettle to talk about it and we hope that you'll join us. Thanks for coming on, guys, and we'll talk soon. ®

#9928. Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk

No reopening date as orders face delays and some customers are told to refuse deliveries to cancel purchases

Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders.

The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation.

Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access.

Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns.

The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers.

Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity.

There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised.

It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion.

Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed.

Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected.

Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer.

The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

#9927. Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one agent loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

You have an agent that can already record a demonstration and push it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every new checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. It covered the Robot() factory, recording a demonstration in simulation, running a policy, and deploying the same agent code to a physical SO-101. That factory resolves a name against a registry of arms, humanoids, mobile bases, and hands, so the SO-100 used throughout this post is one of many supported embodiments. The robot catalog lists every robot the factory knows about. LeRobot's dataset format is already used by over 90,000 datasets and models on the Hub from more than 8,000 publishers (LeRobot Project Pulse). A Strands Robots recording is one more of them, so anything built to read LeRobot data can read it without conversion. If you are new to Strands Robots, start there; this post assumes that setup.

That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for. This post walks you through the data loop inside a single agent: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at examples/notebooks/05_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the agent you build here records a LeRobotDataset from a natural-language prompt, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back in the same process that wrote it: the same Strands Robots Robot() that recorded the dataset streams it. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so100") records a LeRobotDataset through the shared DatasetRecorder; sync_dataset_to_bucket(...) syncs it into a Storage Bucket; stream_dataset(...) reads it back over the Hub with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with mode="real". The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

Because one Robot() both records a dataset and reads it back, collecting data and training on it are two methods on one object over one backend. The agent decides to run an episode and invokes one tool; the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the trained policy producing every action. The whole loop, in a handful of lines:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a mock policy, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Your agent records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. Record the episode, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The prompt asks for the mock policy, a stand-in that produces joint actions without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id defaults to the dataset directory name. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

sync_dataset_to_bucket(root, bucket, run_id=...) validates the dataset and syncs it through the hf CLI, decoupled from the recording lifecycle. The same capability is on DatasetRecorder.sync_to_bucket(bucket, run_id=...) if you drive an open recorder directly, and stop_recording(bucket=...) syncs at the moment you stop an active recording. The bucket is the working layer you write to through the day; for the versioned, published artifact you still call push_to_hub(). Both hold the same format.

The episode is structurally complete, but the actions are placeholders, so it is not training data you would want. Swap in a real policy with create_policy("") for actual grasping; the prompt, the format, and the bucket sync stay identical.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync call takes it to a bucket: sync_dataset_to_bucket("./recordings", "my-org/robot-fave", run_id="run-021") (or the hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021 CLI it wraps). Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a new file only when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. So a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and Strands Robots exposes it through stream_dataset():

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; stream_dataset() reads batches straight from the bucket with nothing on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes, and the training step itself is the ordinary PyTorch one:

If you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset your agent collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:

Buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. Reach for stream_dataset() when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop. For proprioceptive-only streaming, drop_videos=True skips video decode entirely, which is what makes this work on an edge device with no torchcodec wheel. The recording and datasets guide documents that argument along with the delta_timestamps map it requires.

Provider names are shared between running a policy and training one. create_trainer("lerobot_local") returns a Trainer that works like create_policy(), and a TrainSpec describes the run; the record-train-deploy loop then closes in a few lines:

On a single NVIDIA L4 (g6.4xlarge), 500 optimizer steps of ACT (51.6M parameters, effective batch size 8) over a 120-frame episode completed in 133 seconds and wrote a checkpoint that create_policy() loads back through the same entry point used to run any other policy. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, so treat this as one measured configuration rather than a benchmark. The "groot" and "cosmos3" providers target the same TrainSpec and Trainer lifecycle, so the surrounding loop is unchanged; each one validates its own required fields first, so a GR00T run needs a base_model and an embodiment tag, and a Cosmos 3 run needs a base_model and an SFT recipe. Call trainer.validate(spec) before train() and it returns the exact list of what a given backend is missing.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise plans, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions announced as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

On macOS, import strands_robots puts Homebrew's ffmpeg on the loader path for you, so torchcodec decodes streamed video without extra setup.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post, with one keyword argument changed to mode="real":

The checkpoint runs against the physical arm, and the demonstrations that arm records are saved to disk in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), none of the format work in this post changes. A LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, so it stores on Amazon S3 the same as anywhere else, and the recording, training, and deploy steps read that format wherever it sits. What a bucket adds is the Hub-native route: sync_dataset_to_bucket and stream_dataset(repo_type="bucket") target hf:// directly, so you get the sync and the streaming read with no separate storage path to wire up. Both paths run the same loop: Amazon S3 if that is where your data already sits, a bucket if you want the sync and the streaming read without provisioning storage first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you are recording into that bucket, syncing only the bytes that changed, and streaming those bytes to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format, and it never leaves the Hub.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in examples/notebooks/05_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, render, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the mock policy, so no GPU, no Docker, and no Hugging Face credentials are needed.

Run the cells top to bottom. The recorded dataset lands under /tmp/nb5_dataset. To sync it to a bucket, set BUCKET = "my-org/robot-fave" in the first cell (after hf auth login); the neighboring RUN_ID names the folder inside the bucket, and the notebook streams back from f"{BUCKET}/{RUN_ID}". To train on a GPU, raise steps to 500 and set device="cuda". The agent-driven version of the same loop lives at examples/06_agent_collect_and_stream.py.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots and now also write to and read from shared storage, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions or overwrite bucket contents.

Training data is a trust boundary. An agent that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Bucket credentials and scope. sync_dataset_to_bucket(...), stop_recording(bucket=...), and sync_to_bucket upload through the hf CLI using the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you push_to_hub and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Pass an explicit run_id per collection run, as in sync_dataset_to_bucket("./recordings", "my-org/robot-fave", run_id="run-021"). For anything you need to be able to return to, push_to_hub() to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. The local inference path loads Hugging Face models with trust_remote_code=True. Set STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1 to opt in, and only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. When loading pre-trained weights from the Hub (e.g., via pretrained_name_or_path), verify the organization is trusted before loading. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

The loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, substitute its RUN_ID (nb5_demo by default) for cube_pick. Anything you published with push_to_hub() is in a versioned repository and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policy providers, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording and datasets guide documents the DatasetRecorder API, sync_dataset_to_bucket / sync_to_bucket, and stream_dataset in full.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time. The recording and datasets guide describes how to train across several of them.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, the TrainSpec and Trainer lifecycle from Step 3 covers GR00T and Cosmos 3 behind their own provider names, so fine-tuning a VLA on the dataset you just streamed is the same calls with a different provider string and a base model. Running the result is where the paths diverge, because a VLA checkpoint deploys to hardware rather than to the simulator you trained from. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (sim-newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot() factory, so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so an agent can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before it records one of its own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an issue with what worked and what didn't.

Explore robot demonstration data with an interactive dashboard

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. #9926. Who can still open your files after they've left?

EVENT: Peers compare how they find the shares nobody closed, over dinner with The Register in London.

Someone left your organisation in the spring. Can they still open the project share? Most infrastructure leads would want to check before answering, and that pause is the subject of a dinner The Register and LucidLink are hosting for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair.

The trouble is the copies. A busy folder lives on the file server, in a sync client, on a couple of laptops and in the share set up for an agency last year, and each copy carries its own permissions. Locking down one leaves the others as they were. Then there's the tool a team built for itself because the approved one was too slow, which IT may not know exists.

The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, and that's what makes it worth going. People say what actually happened in their own shop and how they caught it. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers round the table. Nobody presents.

The talk moves on to unstructured data that keeps growing, the duplicate storage that comes with it, and how to get access back under control without throwing out the storage and governance you've already paid for.

Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited.

InfoQ Homepage News GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform

Nov 06, 2026 3 min read

GitLab 19.5, released on October 15, puts agentic software development and governance at the centre of the platform, making its GitLab MCP server generally available while expanding how external AI agents can interact with GitLab.

The release allows MCP-compatible tools such as Claude Code and Cursor to access GitLab's broader tool catalogue and invoke GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows. At the same time, GitLab is adding controls for governing those external agents, giving security teams visibility into which agents are being used, by whom, and against which projects.

The generally available GitLab MCP server provides agents with access to GitLab capabilities through the Model Context Protocol. New tools allow agents to discover groups, inspect individual CI/CD artifact files, and start or monitor GitLab Duo agents and flows. Administrators can also select which MCP toolsets are exposed, reducing unnecessary tools and the context they consume.

Giving an agent every available tool increases both context consumption and the number of actions the model could potentially take. Toolset selection provides a relatively simple form of least-privilege agent design.

GitLab.com also introduces MCP rate limits of 60 requests per minute for Free users and 600 for Premium and Ultimate users, with reconnects and retries counting towards the limit.

One of the more significant additions is the ability to bring Externally Connected Agents into GitLab's AI Governance capabilities.

Previously, the AI Governance Dashboard focused on GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents. GitLab 19.5 allows tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex to be connected through the GitLab CLI. Once configured, organisations can record qualifying agent sessions, including the user, agent, project, and timing, with activity appearing alongside GitLab's own agents. Audit events can also be streamed to a SIEM.

This is an important step beyond simply providing an MCP endpoint. Connectivity creates capability; governance determines whether that capability can be safely used at organisational scale.

GitLab Duo CLI also gains an auto mode, allowing agents to execute tools without requesting approval for every shell command, Git operation, or MCP call. The feature is disabled by default and can be controlled at instance, group, and project levels, while tools explicitly marked Always Deny remain blocked.

The /goal command is also now generally available, allowing developers to describe an open-ended objective and have GitLab Duo delegate implementation and verification to a governed flow.

Together, these features move GitLab closer to an agent operating model in which developers provide intent while agents execute multiple steps across the development environment.

That makes the governance controls increasingly important: the more autonomous the agent becomes, the less practical it is to rely on a human approving every individual action.

The release also makes GitLab Secrets Manager generally available. Built on OpenBao, it integrates with existing GitLab group and project permissions, scopes secrets to the jobs that require them, and generates audit events for secret operations.

GitLab is also expanding security configuration profiles, allowing organisations to centrally customise settings such as excluded paths, analyzer images and full-history scans for Secret Detection and SAST rather than repeating configuration in every project's CI/CD file.

These changes complement the agent features by strengthening the controls around the repositories, credentials, and pipelines that agents may access.

GitLab's direction increasingly resembles GitHub's strategy of turning coding agents into participants in the software lifecycle, but GitLab is placing particular emphasis on connecting external agents to its existing DevSecOps governance model.

GitHub's ecosystem benefits from the reach of GitHub Copilot and coding agents, while tools such as Cursor and Claude Code focus more heavily on the developer's local environment. GitLab's MCP approach instead attempts to make the DevOps platform itself agent-accessible, including repositories, issues, pipelines, artifacts, and GitLab-native agents.

The competitive question GitLab is looking at is moving beyond which coding assistant generates better code to which platform provides the safest and most useful environment for autonomous agents to perform engineering work.

#9924. State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

In the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

There used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

The chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

That leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

The two organizations publishing the most new open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

When smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

More hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

At the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

AMD contributed many conversions. This work is important: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

We took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

We counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

The two numbers record different acts. A like says a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it currently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

China's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

The difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, shows the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an important role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

If frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below shows a different story.

Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses

DeepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

Whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

Qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 new repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual launches. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

These factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future users.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

Among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

So how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

In February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most important project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

The ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

And that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

Model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

Across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

We could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

Claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

The second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen new client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

We spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

However, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the big models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future users. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

This article was edited to include latest releases in early August.
