#9923. Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways

Missing DMARC or wobbly SPF means your mail may be treated as suspicious

A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.

The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.

Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.

Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).

The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.

A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.

Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.

It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

#9922. systemd loves Rust

By Christian Brauner and Lennart Poettering

systemd recently merged support for Rust. Going forward it will be possible to write systemd components in Rust in addition to C.

The choice to integrate another core language into a large and established project is always contentious. We have seen the same when Rust was adopted as an additional language for the Linux kernel. As we know by now, that has mostly been successful.

Rust support in systemd has two possible meanings:

The project came to the conclusion that (1) is acceptable while (2) is (currently) not, as the scope and requirements are very different between these two options.

Option (2) is complicated. The details are best left to another blog post but the gist is that we require first-class shared library support in Rust. In the Rust community, this is often referred to as the “stable ABI problem,” which is a well-known and long-standing issue. Until that is available we cannot integrate Rust into root components, otherwise every shared library and many binaries would be bloated by duplicated Rust code.

Static linking for a project like systemd that is split into many tiny components (> 180 binaries currently) is simply not practical or desirable. Generally, static linking works for the leaves of the OS but the core often has different requirements.

Option (1) means that the shared code remains C-only, and we wrap this functionality as Rust crates. The crates are then used for Rust binaries. This allows us to consume all the core API functions uniformly across all components independent of whether they are written in Rust or in C.

When Rust was accepted into systemd, the project adopted the following principles:

Uniform Access to Core APIs. The systemd shared library has a wide range of helpers that provide features and security that are far beyond what either libc or any Rust crate provide.

The clearest example is systemd’s chase*() family of functions. It is a purely fd-based API for path lookup that the whole tree uses. Any new kernel feature that improves on the security and reliability of path lookup is immediately adopted and securely abstracted. There is no equivalent to any of this in core Rust.

Uniform Behavior. Binaries in C and in Rust look and behave identically in how they parse options, display help, and output error messages.

It is inherently unacceptable for binaries in Rust to spuriously differ from systemd’s C binaries. The user should never have to care about the specific language a binary is implemented in. It simply shouldn’t affect behavior.

Uniform Build System. Like most contemporary programming languages, Rust comes with its own build and dependency management ecosystem: cargo. Much like the kernel, systemd explicitly chose not to rely on cargo to build Rust.

systemd uses meson as its build system and integrating a second build system next to it would be a bad idea in our opinion and a great way of complicating the lives of distribution maintainers.

The security and supply-chain attack issues associated with cargo have been raised as a concern as well.

Controlled Dependencies. systemd maintains strictly loose dependencies on other projects. Nowadays, systemd links exclusively against libc. Every other dependency is provided via dlopen() using ELF notes to mark the dependencies.

Accepting a new dependency is a careful process and involves vetting the individual projects in terms of maintenance and security.

While systemd doesn’t oppose the usage of external crates in principle, it is intentionally conservative in not accepting any dependency on them until the project has had some experience with the wider Rust ecosystem and community.

No-std Rust. systemd also doesn’t use the Rust standard library. We currently don’t need to consume anything that the standard library provides. To reiterate an earlier point by way of example, none of the path lookup functionality provided by Rust is currently acceptable in the security sensitive system components provided by systemd.

Fallible Allocations. Failing allocations in Rust cause panics. systemd always treats allocations as fallible and handles them gracefully whenever possible. So systemd provides its own allocator crate that makes memory handling across the whole systemd codebase uniform. Again, much like the kernel does.

No Gratuitous Rewrites. Long-established and reliable parts of the codebase written in C will not be converted without good reason.

If new languages have one downside it is that they cause rewrites of established and stable projects for the sake of using the language rather than solving an actual problem.

One of the clearest examples is rewrites of components whose inherent attack surface is path-based lookup instead of memory safety. Projects ported to another language need more than a bug-for-bug compatible rewrite to actually benefit from the rewrite. It’s far more important to focus on removing their core attack surface.

Rust Remains Optional. The feature set available to existing users will not regress. We’re aware that Rust does not (yet) support all possible architectures, and there are places where introducing Rust would be complicated, so for now at least, Rust remains optional, and systemd without Rust remains fully usable and supported.

Integrating Rust into systemd is an ongoing process. It is exciting to see where the many maintainers of the project are going to take it and how this will evolve. Rust is a good language. Its syntax is a matter of acquired taste and learning but it does bring a range of features to the table that an established project wants to use. One of the systemd maintainers recently discovered that his work on adopting Fibers in systemd naturally integrates with Rust in a surprisingly elegant way.

systemd would also like to see Rust adopted in core components and is willing to engage with the Rust community to make this a reality. The hope is that adopting Rust, even if only in leaf binaries for now, sends another strong signal to the Rust community that core components of the Linux stack are adopting Rust. It would be nice if fundamental blockers such as the lack of first-class support for shared libraries or the ability to interact with the file system primarily through file descriptors were addressed.

It was already an encouraging sign when the Rust community quickly reverted a change in Rust 1.100 that would’ve broken the newly merged Rust support in systemd. This is much appreciated and it is great to see that the community is paying attention. The systemd project is paying attention too!

#9921. Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

An unknown operator appears to have exfiltrated SQL Server backups from the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration in under a half hour.

An unknown threat actor managed to gain access to sensitive databases belonging to the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, exfiltrating nearly 69GB of information on workers, contracts, and financial records, according to an analysis of a staging server used in the breach.

Over 24 minutes, the attacker copied 27 backup databases with information on overseas-employment case management, including accreditation, contracts, and cashier and LandBank records, according to threat intelligence firm Hunt.io's Oct. 28 analysis of the logs found on a Singaporean staging server used by the attacker. The cyberattackers used privileged escalation tools, namely GodPotato and SeImpersonate, and the Impacket network library for Python to move the data, but the trail stopped at the staging server, says Esteban Borges, head of research for Hunt.io.

The server had been accessed later, but by whom is not clear, Borges says. While Hunt.io has not yet discovered the data as advertised for sale, the information may have been detected and removed, but that seems unlikely, he says.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

"I won't claim the backups stopped on the staging server," he says, so it's "still a breach, since the data was copied out of the agency’s control and the log shows the transfer completing."

This is not the first time that cybersecurity firms have found evidence that Philippine government data had been stolen. In August, Hunt.io discovered another threat actor's workspace hosting a number of tools and, in that case, 1.2GB of data stolen from a Philippine nuclear regulatory agency and a maritime shipbuilding contractor. A year ago, Philippine police arrested the mayor of a small town after discovering she was a Chinese national posing as a Filipina citizen and operating a cyber-scam center.

Whether the current incident involved China or cybercriminal groups is not clear. While Hunt.io did find some Chinese language fragments in the parts of the code, that code belonged to a third-party software library; thus, Hunt.io did not attribute the hack. The company did say, however, that both cybercriminals and nation-state adversaries would find value in the personally identifiable information (PII).

"That kind of migrant-worker PII, plus contract and payment data, is useful for fraud and identity theft, so it has commercial value," Borges says. "It's also a detailed map of a diaspora population, which can interest a state actor."

The latest insight into attacks on the Philippine government came after Hunt.io researchers discovered an open directory on a server hosted on the Singaporean address space of a Helsinki-based firm, UpCloud Ltd., the analysis stated. The open directory contained tools and log files for the attack, including a rebranded version of the GodPotato privilege escalation library, a PowerShell stager to unpack tools in memory, and the full Impacket Python environment.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

While Hunt.io considered the incident a confirmed compromise, the lack of runtime telemetry meant that Borges could not answer where the attacker moved the data.

"[W]e still can’t answer ... how they got in, whether the payload ran, and where the data went," he says.

However, the tools and the attacker's process indicated an operator with some strong ability, but who also made some simple mistakes, Borges says.

"The payload engineering is competent, [but] the operational security is poor — they left the staging server and its logs wide open," he says. "[It was] someone who can build the tool properly but was careless about keeping their own server quiet. I wouldn't call that top-tier or amateur."

The impact of the breach may boil down to the identity of the attacker and what they do with the stolen data. While Hunt.io notified the CERT Philippines (CERT-PH) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), the company declined to provide any more details of the national responses to the leak.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

However, Borges did say that, so far, the information has not appeared for sale on the Dark Web.

"We haven't seen the backups surface for sale or in a leak," he says. "We never opened the backups themselves."

Governments in the region need to scan their own networks and lock down their attack surface area, he says. Workers with too many privileges allow attackers with tools such as SeImpersonate to gain more access to assets on the network. Hunt.io also found that the migrant-worker portal exposed a number of risky ports, including SMB on 445 and WinRM on 5985 and 47001.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9920. Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

We built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

One note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

"Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

Two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

The reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

The ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

The two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

It is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario]

Across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.)

The allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

Utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

In the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

The alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:

The objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

The relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

It is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

The time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, new jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

That heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

That design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

The system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

The uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

Everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

Training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

Quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

Real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

This closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

The obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

The failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

The architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the plan for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

The consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive plans update rather than thrash.

There is a secondary payoff. The horizon plan is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

This is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

The same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

The previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

The GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.

#9919. Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Organizations may not be ready for completely autonomous communication processes, but there are places where automating information updates would alleviate pressure.

Organizations steadily deploy automated threat detection and response processes; some even take it a step further with fully artificial intelligence (AI) security operations centers (SOCs). Automation can catch an incident in seconds, yet communication remains mostly manual across an industry that requires more transparency.

The disconnect can strain relationships and trust as customers wait for incident impact and mitigation answers. Hands-on communications also put more pressure on chief information security officers (CISOs), who must relay timely updates to IT personnel and executives as the incident clock winds down.

Incident response (IR) communications are increasingly too much for humans to coordinate without more help. But disclosures contain sensitive information — the status of a company's security posture or how they responded when alerted to an incident — and automation takes away some of the control leadership wants to hold onto in regard to timing and specifics.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

From a coordination and information standpoint, automating communications is absolutely important, says Tim Brown, chief strategy officer at Cytactic. That could mean implementing a centralized place to view everyone's status versus relying on meetings to receive updates.

A dedicated crisis communication platform could help, Brown says. A single click of a button could notify everyone, and that includes contingency options if normal communications go down, which is typical following an incident where systems go offline.

Brown is no stranger to hectic IR communication scenarios. While trying to manage the SolarWinds attack fallout, the former CISO got pulled into one crisis after the other. He oversaw five different teams, coordinated tasks, scheduled meetings, received updates from everyone, and tried to keep the customers briefed.

As he looks back now, he appreciates how much help everyone around him was. Still, some preparation was missing: more tabletop exercises, meeting the appropriate people beforehand, and technology to ease communications.

IR communications are complicated. Organizations may wait to disclose certain information, so they do not tip off attackers. Sometimes victim organizations post customer-only private advisories, but that leaves public awareness and downstream victims vulnerable. Yet other times, companies simply choose not to disclose or downplay effects to save face.

The Securities and Exchange Commission and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) continue to update and adopt new disclosure regulations in light of more disruptive attacks. The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) of 2022, after missing several earlier deadlines, is nearing finalization. Once in effect, the rule would require covered entities to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours of discovery, and critical infrastructure organizations that make ransom payments would need to report within 24 hours.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Even if organizations want to disclose any information in good faith, that poses challenges. A wide net of victims, third parties, and supply chain risks abound. It's increasingly more difficult to even know who is affected these days.

Douglas McKee, director of vulnerability intelligence at Rapid7, ventures to guess that most security leaders would cite communication problems, and they usually exist long before an incident ever happens. For example, security teams tend to talk in terms of common vulnerability exposures (CVEs) and indicators of compromise, while the people making business decisions need to know what any of that actually means.

On a normal day, that gap is annoying, but during an incident, the language barrier gets amplified because everyone needs answers at the same moment, even though the facts change by the hour. And nobody wants to be the person who said the wrong thing publicly, McKee adds.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

"Third parties make this even harder," he tells Dark Reading. "I've seen plenty of situations where a vendor knows about a problem in their product well before their customers do, but the notification lands in a generic inbox or goes to a contact who left the company two years ago.”

Attackers benefit from that confusion, he notes, adding how important it is for defenders to agree internally on what's happening so they can relay information to customers confidently.

Organizations want to be more transparent but continually struggle with how to personalize communication outreach, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Whether in day-to-day fraud communications or during an active incident, the more they can leverage AI, insights, and understanding the better they can adapt, he adds .

Right now, it's easier to automate detection and response because the inputs can be fairly structured, explains McKee; a log entry either matches a rule or it doesn't. IR communication, on the other hand, involves judgement calls with legal and reputational consequences.

"Organizations are understandably nervous about letting a machine decide what goes out the door with their name on it," McKee says. "Let's face it: An analyst can shrug off a false positive in a few minutes, but there's no easy way to 'unsend' an inaccurate breach notice to your customers."

That doesn't mean automating communication is off the table — it just needs to be pointed at the right parts of the problem, he says. Organizations can automate pulling together the incident timeline or tracking which stakeholders have been notified and when. McKee also recommends using tools to draft a first version of an update from data the responders already have.

It's all about freeing people up to spend their time on decisions that actually need a human. The way McKee looks at it, "automation should get the draft in front of the right person faster, and that person should still be the one who verifies and hits send."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9918. The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't

Infrastructure spending outruns measurable returns, with supplier finances key to judging when trouble arrives

The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices.

Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash.

"Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins.

"About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs."

Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare.

Its latest report, "An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register, have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use.

At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value.

A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity.

Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models.

If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist.

Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course.

Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says.

Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost.

But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains."

Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections.

Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.

Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

#9917. A C++ Quicksort Faster Than std::sort

blqsort is a very fast quicksort algorithm. I am not aware of any other general-purpose comparison-based sorting algorithm that is faster on random data. Only specialized SIMD-based algorithms are generally faster when dealing with small primitive data types.

The main ideas are branchless partitioning, sorting networks for small partitions and robust pivot selection.

The implementation is available on GitHub under the MIT license. There is also a C version of it, including multithreaded versions, each as a single header file.

The following benchmarks show the execution times for sorting 50 million random doubles using different sorting implementations. The measurements were taken on an Apple M1 system using Clang and on an Intel i5-9300H Linux system using GCC, both compiled with the -O3 option.

For a fair comparison, the single-threaded version of blqs was used here. On the M1, the multithreaded versions are roughly another factor of 3 faster. In terms of runtime, the C versions differ only very little from the C++ version.

Execution times for sorting 50 million of these structs with random id values.

struct entry { int id; int value; bool operator<(const entry& other) const { return id < other.id; } }; struct entry data[SIZE]; blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE);

Already sorted and reverse-sorted inputs are detected and handled efficiently. Inputs with many duplicate keys are optimized as well.

The execution times, unless otherwise specified, apply to an Apple M1 system.

#include #include #include constexpr int SIZE = 50000000; double data[SIZE]; double time() { static auto time0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); auto t = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); std::chrono::duration diff = t - time0; return diff.count(); } void sortq(double ar[], int len) { if (len < 2) return; double piv = ar[0]; int mid = 0; for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) { if (ar[i] < piv) { mid += 1; std::swap(ar[mid], ar[i]); } } std::swap(ar[mid], ar[0]); sortq(ar + mid + 1, len - mid - 1); sortq(ar, mid); } int main() { double t0; printf("Sorting %d million doubles\n", SIZE / 1000000); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = rand() / 1024.0; t0 = time(); sortq(data, SIZE); printf("sortq: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); } c++ -O1 main.cpp && ./a.out Sorting 50 million doubles sortq: 4.61s If you sort the sorted data again, all elements in the partition are greater than or equal to the pivot element. The second partition becomes only one element smaller each time, and the function is called recursively millions of times, which leads to a stack overflow after a few hours.

You can prevent this with tail call elimination. That is, the first recursive call remains, while the second is replaced by a loop iteration. You now need to ensure that the smaller partition is called recursively. So swap them if necessary.

void sortq(double* ar, int len) { while (len >= 2) { double piv = ar[0]; int mid = 0; for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) { if (ar[i] < piv) { mid += 1; std::swap(ar[mid], ar[i]); } } std::swap(ar[mid], ar[0]); double* ar2 = ar + mid + 1; int len2 = len - mid - 1; len = mid; if (len2 > len) { std::swap(len, len2); std::swap(ar, ar2); } sortq(ar2, len2); } } Now the program no longer crashes, but it will take a few days to finish. Because of this unfavorable partitioning, the worst-case scenario of O(N²) has become a reality. However, insertion sort would not make it any faster either.

Let’s just use the middle element as the pivot - then the problem of sorting already sorted data will be gone.

. while (len >= 2) { std::swap(ar[len / 2], ar[0]); double piv = ar[0]; . The only remaining risk is that someone intentionally sends specially crafted data to trigger this behavior. To eliminate this threat, the pivot point should be selected randomly.

This implementation is sufficient for many purposes and is also reasonably fast. By the way, “Lomuto” partitioning is used here. “Hoare” partitioning performs fewer comparisons and swaps, but on modern CPUs its cache behavior can be less favorable.

But why write your own implementation when std::sort exists?

. #include . . t0 = time(); std::sort(data, data + SIZE); printf("std::sort: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); . std::sort: 1.31s That’s on ARM Mac - on a x86 system, std::sort is only about 10% faster.

How can you make a quicksort run faster than std::sort?

For partitions with up to about 20 elements, insertion sort is faster than quicksort. But there is something even faster for small partitions: sorting networks. Each partition size is handled in its own program branch. For a partition size of two, the two elements are simply compared and swapped if necessary. However, as the number of elements increases, the logic becomes increasingly complex.

inline void sort2(double& a, double& b) { if (a < b) std::swap(a, b); } inline void sort3(double& a, double& b, double& c) { sort2(a, b); sort2(b, c); sort2(a, b); } inline void sort4(double& a, double& b, double& c, double& d) { sort2(a, b); sort2(c, d); sort2(a, c); sort2(b, d); sort2(b, c); } inline void sort5(double& a, double& b, double& c, double& d, double& e) { sort2(b, c); sort2(d, e); sort2(b, d); sort2(a, c); sort2(a, d); sort2(c, e); sort2(a, b); sort2(c, d); sort2(b, c); } . while (len >= 6) { . . } if (len == 5) sort5(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2], ar[3], ar[4]); else if (len == 4) sort4(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2], ar[3]); else if (len == 3) sort3(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2]); else if (len == 2) sort2(ar[0], ar[1]); }

Let’s consider a simple task: Iterate through an array and copy all numbers less than 500 into a new array. A straightforward implementation in C looks like this:

smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { if (numbers[i] < 500) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += 1; } } If the numbers are randomly distributed, the result of the if condition becomes unpredictable for the branch predictor. This results in a high misprediction rate, which severely impacts performance because the processor must constantly flush its pipeline and restart execution.

We can avoid this problem by using a branchless approach:

smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += (numbers[i] < 500); } Although this version introduces an unconditional write operation (writing to memory even if the condition is not met), the associated overhead is generally much lower than the performance loss resulting from a branch misprediction.

Branchless does not mean that there are no jumps at all. The term refers only to the comparison, which is difficult to predict. Obviously, the loop jump remains, but that is not a problem because it is easily predictable - it is skipped only once.

To get meaningful results, we run both routines for 1000 iterations using 100,000 random numbers.

#include #include #include #define SIZE 100000 int numbers[SIZE]; int small_numbers[SIZE]; int smlen; double ts(void) { static double t0; struct timeval tv; gettimeofday(&tv, NULL); double h = t0; t0 = tv.tv_sec + tv.tv_usec / 1000000.0; return t0 - h; } void init(void) { srand(1); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) numbers[i] = rand() % 1000; ts(); } void small_if(void) { smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) { if (numbers[i] < 500) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += 1; } } } void small_bl(void) { smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += (numbers[i] < 500); } } int main(void) { init(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) small_if(); printf("Time if: %.3f\n", ts()); init(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) small_bl(); printf("Time bl: %.3f\n", ts()); } Benchmark results were obtained on an Apple M1 with -O1 optimization. On this benchmark, -O3 did not yield additional speedup, only larger generated code.

Time if: 0.345 Time bl: 0.036 Assembly Analysis

Using objdump -d, we can see the difference in how the CPU processes these loops.

With the if version, the compiler generates a conditional branch b.gt.

ldr w13, [x10], #0x4 ; load numbers[i] cmp w13, #0x1f3 ; compare with 499 (0x1f3) b.gt 0x100000678 ; branch if greater (The bottleneck) str w13, [x12, w8, sxtw #2] ; store value in small_numbers[j] add w8, w8, #0x1 ; j += 1 With the branchless version the compiler uses the cinc (conditional increment) instruction.

ldr w13, [x10], #0x4 ; load numbers[i] str w13, [x12, w8, uxtw #2] ; unconditional store to small_numbers[j] cmp w13, #0x1f4 ; compare with 500 cinc w8, w8, lt ; conditional increment (No branch) In this version, there is no jump based on the data. The control flow is perfectly linear, allowing the CPU to use its full pipeline width.

Why doesn’t the compiler optimize the if case automatically?

The compiler doesn’t know the nature of your data. If only a small fraction of numbers were less than 500, the branch version might actually be faster because the predictor would almost always be right.

The branchless version performs a write operation (str) every single time. The compiler cannot safely assume that it is permitted to write to memory if a write operation in the original source code was intended to occur only under a specific condition - for example, to avoid writing past the end of an allocated buffer.

Since quicksort essentially works by dividing the data into large and small numbers, it should be possible to speed it up using this technique.

So, as described above, we can make the partitioning step branchless. (comp is the comparison function):

int h = comp(*left, piv); *lwr = *rwr = *left++; lwr += h; rwr -= !h; We can also make sort2 - the basic operation for the sorting network - branchless:

inline static void sort2(double& a, double& b) { double x = a; double y = b; bool m = x < y; a = m ? x : y; b = m ? y : x; } Here’s how it works (in short) :

First, about 250 elements are copied from one page into an auxiliary buffer to make room for subsequent operations. We then alternately copy a block to the left and to the right, without using any branches.

The pivot element is also carefully selected. Several medians are determined from various elements of the partition, and the final median is then calculated from these medians. This results in a much more even distribution of the data. Some randomness is added to the pivot selection process to prevent inputs from consistently triggering worst-case behavior.

If the distribution is still very uneven, however, the algorithm switches to heap sort for these partitions as a precaution. Uneven distribution often occurs when there are many identical elements; in this case, they are identified and grouped together.

In addition, the code includes the sorting networks, which are used for partition sizes up to 16.

And with a for (int i = 16; i--;) { ... } loop, the compiler unrolls the loop, generating 16 copies of the loop body.

This version consists of a single C++ header file that can be easily included. It can sort any data type, and the comparison function can be supplied by the user, just like with std::sort.

#include #include #include #include "blqs.h" constexpr int SIZE = 50000000; double data[SIZE]; double time() { static auto time0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); auto t = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); std::chrono::duration diff = t - time0; return diff.count(); } int main() { double t0; printf("Sorting %d million doubles\n", SIZE / 1000000); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = rand() / 1024.0; t0 = time(); blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE); printf("blqs::sort: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); } c++ -O3 test.cpp && ./a.out Sorting 50 million doubles blqs::sort: 0.95s std::sort took 1.33. And on x86 systems, it’s now three times as fast as std::sort

Interestingly, this idiomatic C notation is compiled into very efficient, branchless code on ARM-based Macs using the csel command: if (comp(x, piv)) *lwr++ = x; else *rwr-- = x; Surprisingly, this doesn’t work with the more explicit version:

if (comp(x, piv)) { *lwr = x; lwr++; } else { *rwr = x; rwr--; } One would actually expect that the compiler would treat these two variants as equivalent. Many people don’t trust AI to generate good code. Perhaps we shouldn’t blindly trust the compiler either.

This code is generated (on ARM Macs) - but only in the compact if version:

; x9 = current element pointer ; x0 = left destination (grows forwards) ; x20 = right destination (grows backwards); d8 = pivot ; x8 = 8 (positive increment) ; x10 = -8 (negative increment) loop: ldr d0, [x9], #8 fcmp d0, d8 ; compare value against pivot csel x11, x0, x20, mi ; target is left (x0) or right (x20) str d0, [x11] ; store value to the selected destination csel x12, x8, xzr, mi ; left_step is 8 or 0 csel x13, xzr, x10, mi ; right_step is 0 or -8 add x0, x0, x12 ; left += left_step add x20, x20, x13 ; right += right_step b.ls loop So, branchless without that double store.

On x86, it works similarly with Clang. But not with GCC, and not with the longer if version either. It is also slower than the explicit, branchless version.

if (comp(x, piv)) *lwr++ = x; else *sw++ = x; } while (left <= right) { T x = *left++; if (comp(x, piv)) *lwr++ = x; else *sw++ = x; } std::memcpy(lwr, swbuf, (sw - swbuf) * sizeof(T)); lwr -= 1; *outerleft = *lwr; med5(left[1 + j], left[2 + j], left[3 + j], left[4 + j], left[5 + j], comp); med5(left[11 + j], left[12 + j], left[13 + j], left[14 + j], left[15 + j], comp); med5(left[21 + j], left[22 + j], left[23 + j], left[24 + j], left[25 + j], comp); med5(pivp[-2], pivp[-1], piv, pivp[1], pivp[2], comp); med5(right[-24 - j], right[-23 - j], right[-22 - j], right[-21 - j], right[-20 - j], comp); med5(right[-14 - j], right[-13 - j], right[-12 - j], right[-11 - j], right[-10 - j], comp); } template static void smallsort(T* left, T* right, Compare comp) { while (right - left > 15) { T* mid = partition_small(left, right, comp); smallsort(left, mid - 1, comp); left = mid + 1; } sorting_network(left, right - left, comp); } template static void blqsort(T* left, T* right, Compare comp) { while (1) { ptrdiff_t partszm1 = right - left; if (partszm1 <= SMALLPART) break; T* mid = partition_large(left, right, comp); if (mid - left < partszm1 / 16) { if (mid > left) blqsort(left, mid - 1, comp); T piv = *mid; mid += 1; // collect duplicates for (T* p = mid; p <= right; p++) { if (!comp(piv, *p)) { std::swap(*mid, *p); mid++; } } left = mid; if (right - left < SMALLPART) break; // second chance before fallback to heapsort mid = partition_large(left, right, comp); if (mid - left < partszm1 / 16) { if (mid > left) heap_sort(left, mid - 1, comp); if (mid < right) heap_sort(mid + 1, right, comp); return; } } if (mid - left < right - mid) { blqsort(left, mid - 1, comp); left = mid + 1; } else { blqsort(mid + 1, right, comp); right = mid - 1; } } smallsort(left, right, comp); } template > void sort(T* first, T* last, Compare comp = Compare()) { if (last - first < 2) return; blqsort(first, last - 1, comp); } } #endif The 50 million doubles are now sorted on the ARM Mac almost twice as fast as with std::sort.

Sorting 50 million doubles blqs::sort: 0.67s

You only need to include blqs.h, and it can be used just as easily as std::sort.

For the C++ multithreaded variant, which uses C++ threads, include blqs_thr.h instead of blqs.h. The function call remains the same.

In practice, we often need to sort custom data structures. This is where SIMD libraries like Google Highway - while very fast for simple numbers - become difficult to use.

Using std::sort or blqsort gives you much more flexibility.

#include "blqs.h" struct entry { int id; int value; bool operator<(const entry& other) const { return id < other.id; } }; struct entry data[SIZE]; blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE); Depending on the compiler and platform, either the if version or the explicit branchless version is used.

For types with higher copy costs that are not is_trivially_copyable (such as strings), the buffer-based branchless approach becomes less efficient. In such cases, a BlockQuicksort (Edelkamp and Weiß) variant is used instead. This processes only the element indices in a branchless manner. This requires C++17 or later.

c++ -O3 -std=c++17 test_double.cpp && ./a.out
