#9908. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

#9907. What's new in Node.js 27

Node.js 27 brings V8 15.6 with Iterator.zip, Iterator.zipKeyed, Math.sumPrecise, net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, and a 4 GB default heap limit.

On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0. If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release?

Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027.

Wait, an odd-numbered Node.js release becoming LTS?

Yes, the odd/even split is gone. Version numbers now match the calendar year (27 in 2027), with one major release per year, and every release becomes LTS. We covered the timeline and the reasons for the change in Node.js is changing its release schedule and version numbers. Because Node.js 27 is currently in its Alpha window, I will keep updating this article as new builds land on the way to April 2027.

In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), and Math.sumPrecise(). There is a promises API for node:net, along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System (node:vfs) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env, and HTTP and memory defaults change too.

We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading.

Every code block with a file path in its title matches a runnable file in the companion repo lmammino/nodejs-27-examples on GitHub.

For example, we can format a list of products and total their prices:

If you want to experiment locally, check your current Node.js version before running the snippets below.

This is the part of the release I’m most excited about. I love seeing how far we can push streams, iterators, and generators. Our article on JavaScript async iterators should give you an idea of what I mean.

In What’s new in Node.js 26, we used Iterator.concat() to consume multiple iterables one after another. Node.js 27, through V8 15.6, lets us consume them side by side, pairing values at the same position.

Suppose you are checking a weather forecast against the temperatures recorded over the same four days. The predictions come from your model, while the actual values come from observations. To calculate each day’s error, you need to pair the values at the same position. Both sequences must cover the same days in the same order.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, if both sequences were arrays, you would typically use .map() with an index lookup:

That works well for arrays. But what if observations come from a generator, or your model returns an iterator of predictions? Index lookups won’t work on those inputs, and converting them to arrays means loading both sequences into memory first.

In Node.js 27, Iterator.zip() takes an iterable of iterables and returns a lazy iterator of pairs. We can calculate the errors with the same pipeline whether the inputs are arrays or iterators:

Each pair contains a prediction and its corresponding observation. A positive error means the day was warmer than predicted; a negative error means it was cooler. The pairing and mapping happen one item at a time. Only the final .toArray() collects the errors into an array so we can print them together.

Another common use is the dot product of two vectors: multiply matching components, then add the products. This operation appears in graphics, machine learning, and numerical computing:

Here we never collect the pairs or products into an intermediate array. We also use mode: 'strict' because a dot product requires vectors of equal length: silently ignoring extra components would hide an input error.

By default, Iterator.zip() uses { mode: 'shortest' }: it stops when the shortest input finishes and closes the remaining open iterators. For the forecast example, that means comparing only the days available in both sequences. Use { mode: 'strict' } if a missing prediction or observation should instead throw a TypeError. Or pass { mode: 'longest', padding: [null, 0] } to continue until the longest input finishes, using the corresponding padding value when an input runs out.

So far, our inputs have been arrays. But Iterator.zip() also works with iterators that have no end. Imagine a home with two power meters: one measures solar generation, and the other measures household consumption. Each meter gives us its current reading in watts whenever we poll it. Subtracting consumption from generation tells us whether the house has surplus power to export or needs to import power from the grid (assuming there is no battery).

We can wrap each meter in an endless generator. Here we simulate the readings with random values so the example runs without hardware:

Neither generator reads anything until we request a value from netPower. Each request polls both meters once and calculates the difference. Both input iterators can keep producing readings forever, but .take(5) limits this demo to five pairs. Collecting either input with [...solar] or .toArray() would never finish and would eventually exhaust memory.

These are synchronous, on-demand readings: the two meters are polled sequentially, close together, rather than at exactly the same instant. The loop takes five readings immediately; zip() does not add a polling interval. With real hardware, the callbacks would read the meters instead of generating random numbers.

Tuple arrays like [prediction, observation] are easy to read for two or three items, but once you have four or five parallel sources, positional destructuring gets easy to mix up.

Iterator.zipKeyed() accepts an object whose values are iterables. Each step yields an object with the same keys, so you can refer to values by name instead of position:

If an API returns each field as a separate array, like user IDs, names, and roles, Iterator.zipKeyed() lets you process them together as a lazy sequence of row objects. The arrays must describe the same records in the same order.

In Node.js 26, a common way to format a lazy iterator pipeline as a string was to call .toArray().join(', ') at the end. The final .toArray() allocated an array of strings that .join() consumed and discarded.

V8 15.6 adds two terminal helpers directly onto Iterator.prototype:

For join(), let’s return to our sensor readings. This time we only need one temperature sensor, and we want to format five readings as a comma-separated string. As before, we simulate the hardware so you can run the example locally:

.take(5) makes the endless source finite, .map() formats each reading, and .join() builds the string without collecting an intermediate array. These five readings are taken immediately, with no delay between them. Without .take(5), joining this endless iterator would never finish.

For includes(), imagine checking whether a commit message references a particular issue. String.prototype.matchAll() already returns an iterator, so we can extract the complete references and search them directly:

includes() stops as soon as it finds APP-142, without extracting the later reference. Matching complete references also avoids the false positive you would get from message.includes('APP-14'), which matches part of APP-142. The search consumes the iterator, so create a fresh one for another search.

The iterator helpers shown above work with synchronous iterators. Their .next() calls return results directly; these helpers do not await promises from async iterators. You cannot use the same chains on an async function* generator or a Node.js readable stream’s async iterator. Use for await...of or a library with async iterator helpers for those sources. Async iterator helpers are covered by a separate TC39 proposal and are not built into Node.js 27 as of v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0.

Beyond iterator helpers, V8 15.6 also brings a useful addition for numerical calculations: Math.sumPrecise(). To see why it matters, let’s look at a familiar floating-point surprise.

When you sum numbers with .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0), each addition rounds its intermediate result to the nearest representable 64-bit float. Over dozens or thousands of additions, those tiny rounding errors accumulate. Worse, if you add a small number (0.1) to a huge number (1e20) and later add -1e20, the 0.1 is lost completely during the first addition because a 64-bit float doesn’t have enough mantissa bits to hold both magnitudes at once.

In Node.js 27, V8 15.6 enables Math.sumPrecise() by default. It accepts any iterable of numbers, computes the sum using an internal high-precision accumulator, and rounds only once at the very end:

Math.sumPrecise() accepts any iterable, so it also works with the iterators from the previous section. You can pass the result of .map() directly into Math.sumPrecise() without calling .toArray() first:

When you still need integer cents or decimal libraries

Math.sumPrecise() avoids rounding after each addition. Its result is what you would get by adding the exact mathematical values of the input floating-point numbers, then rounding the total once to the nearest representable 64-bit float. But those inputs may already differ from the decimal values you intended:

As the MDN explanation points out, the literals 0.1 and 0.2 are stored as binary floating-point values slightly greater than their exact decimal counterparts. Adding those stored values and rounding once still produces 0.30000000000000004. The method cannot recover the intended decimal inputs.

For money calculations that require exact decimal arithmetic, use integer minor units (like cents) or a decimal library with explicit rounding rules. Math.sumPrecise() improves summation accuracy; it does not turn JavaScript numbers into decimal numbers.

The core node:net module gets iterator support too.

For years, node:fs, node:dns, node:stream, node:timers, and node:readline have all had .promises sub-modules. Yet node:net remained purely callback- and event-driven. If you wanted to spin up a TCP server on an ephemeral port in a test or connect a client socket using async/await, you had to wrap 'listening', 'connect', and 'error' events by hand.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, setting up a TCP server and client with async/await looked like this:

Node.js 27 introduces the experimental node:net/promises module with two helpers, listen() and connect(), and makes net.Server itself an async iterable.

Let’s try something fun and build a small TCP chat server. Each connected client can send a line of text, and the server forwards it to every other client, prefixed with the sender’s connection ID:

Then open two or three other terminals and run this command in each (with netcat installed):

Each terminal receives its connection ID, for example Connected as 127.0.0.1:54321. Type a message and press Enter. The other terminals receive a line such as 127.0.0.1:54321 > Hello everyone!. The server does not echo messages back to their sender. Press Ctrl+C in a client terminal to disconnect, or in the server terminal to close the chat and all active connections.

With three netcat clients connected, each terminal receives the other clients’ messages:

listen() resolves once the server is listening. The clients map tracks active sockets by their remote address and port, which distinguish connections to this server. These are connection labels, not permanent user identities: reconnecting can give a client a different port.

Inside each handler, readline turns the socket’s byte stream into lines. TCP chunks do not correspond to messages: a line may arrive in several chunks, or one chunk may contain several lines. Each completed line is broadcast to every other active socket. The finally block removes disconnected clients and closes their resources.

The outer connection loop starts each handleConnection(socket) call without awaiting it. That lets it accept the next client while earlier handlers wait for messages. Each handler still awaits its own incoming lines, so clients can remain connected and chat concurrently. The .catch() handles rejected handler promises; socket errors are handled separately, and server.maxConnections = 10 caps open connections for this demo.

The pitfall: awaiting each connection handler

This small change would break the chat’s concurrency:

handleConnection() stays active until its client disconnects. Awaiting it here means only the first client gets a handler and joins the clients map. Later connections can be accepted by the server, but the loop will not dispatch their handlers until that first client leaves. There is nobody else in the map to receive the first client’s messages!

The server iterator documentation warns that a slow consumer can buffer connections without bound. Set server.maxConnections explicitly and choose a limit appropriate to your workload, including when dispatching handlers concurrently.

The iterator yields TCP connections, not individual chat messages or application-level requests. Awaiting a handler can be appropriate for deliberate sequential processing, but a chat server needs overlapping connection handlers.

Testing code that reads configuration files often means mocking node:fs or creating temporary directories and cleaning them up afterward. Bundling assets or templates into an archive poses a related problem: how can your application read them through its usual node:fs calls?

The new node:vfs (Virtual File System) module was originally introduced behind --experimental-vfs, and in Node.js 27 it is unflagged and available out of the box (though still marked Experimental Stability 1 while the API settles).

With node:vfs, you can create an isolated, in-memory file system with vfs.create(), populate it using standard fs-style methods, and mount it so regular node:fs operations (and import / require()) can read from it directly. VirtualFileSystem also supports Explicit Resource Management (using), which unmounts it when execution leaves the block:

The using declaration tells JavaScript to call memoryFs[Symbol.dispose]() when execution leaves the block, including when an error is thrown. VirtualFileSystem implements that method to unmount itself. Declaring it with const would require us to call unmount() explicitly.

memoryFs.mount() mounts the virtual file system under a reserved namespace (path.join(os.devNull, 'vfs'), such as /dev/null/vfs/1 on POSIX), so a virtual mount can never accidentally shadow or overwrite real files on your disk. If you want to compare this with working on real files, check out our guide on reading and writing files in Node.js.

You can also use node:vfs through --vfs-load on the CLI without an experimental flag:

That command mounts the companion repo’s 04-vfs/bundle directory and runs its index.js, which prints Hello from the VFS bundle. You can also pass a ZIP archive; Node.js runs its package.json "main" or index.js entry point from the mounted archive. And if you use Single Executable Applications (SEA), vfsArchive is now mounted at layer 0 and automatically available inside Worker threads too.

There are changes across the standard library too, from temporary files to HTTP server defaults.

Until now, if you needed a temporary file in Node.js, your safest built-in option was fs.mkdtemp() to create a temporary directory, and then opening a file inside it. Creating a random filename yourself and calling fs.open() was error-prone and required a retry loop in case of collisions.

Node.js 27 adds APIs modeled on POSIX mkstemp(3): fs.mkstemp(), fs.mkstempSync(), and fsPromises.mkstemp(). It atomically generates a unique filename (appending six random characters to your prefix) and opens the file in a single step, returning both the path and the open FileHandle (or file descriptor fd):

The built-in fs.glob() (introduced in Node.js 22) was ported from JavaScript to native C++ in Node.js 27. The maintainers’ benchmarks show substantial speedups for some workloads, but gains vary by API and options, and one synchronous exclude-pattern workload regressed. Benchmark your own patterns before assuming a speedup.

As we covered in our guide to environment variables in Node.js, process.env is where most applications keep their most sensitive secrets (API keys, database URLs, signing tokens). It is also the very first place a compromised dependency looks when trying to exfiltrate credentials.

Node.js 27 adds --allow-env to the Permission Model (--permission). When --permission is enabled, every environment variable not explicitly matched by --allow-env is scrubbed at process startup before any JavaScript runs (except runtime variables like PATH, HOME, LANG, and NODE_OPTIONS, plus variables explicitly loaded via --env-file):

Node.js also scrubs disallowed variables from the underlying OS environment block and restricts access to /proc/self/environ on Linux. Native code loaded by Node.js sees the reduced environment too. This reduces accidental exposure; the Permission Model is not a sandbox for malicious code. You can remove a variable after reading it with process.permission.drop('env', 'VARIABLE_NAME'). Keep NODE_ENV explicitly if your application uses it, since it is not preserved by default.

The built-in node:test runner has three updates:

These three HTTP changes affect production web servers:

If you are curious why this change was made: it seems a bit weird on the surface, right? Why would Node.js remove the prototype from an otherwise ordinary object?

req.headers is a dictionary: the keys are header names chosen by whoever sent the request, and the values are whatever they sent. An ordinary JavaScript object is a poor fit for that kind of data, because it inherits properties from Object.prototype that have nothing to do with what you stored in it:

Our empty ordinary object already “has” a constructor, inherited from its prototype. __proto__ is even more surprising: Object.prototype defines an accessor with that name, so reading it returns the prototype, and assigning to it tries to change the prototype instead of storing a value. Both names are already lowercase, which matters here because Node.js lowercases incoming header names. A client can send a constructor or __proto__ header, and it arrives under exactly that key.

Notice that the example uses __proto__ in two different ways. { __proto__: null } is special object-literal syntax that creates the object with no prototype at all (Object.create(null) does the same thing, and the new Node.js code uses the literal form). The later headers['__proto__'] = ... is an ordinary assignment: with no inherited __proto__ setter to intercept it, it simply stores an own property, like any other key.

That’s the motivation in PR #62900, by Matteo Collina. Besides consistency with the *Distinct APIs, its commit message says the change “Fixes prototype pollution concerns where headers like __proto__ could be interpreted as prototype manipulation.” My reading is that the goal is clean dictionary semantics: a key exists in req.headers only if the request sent it.

The March 2026 security releases already included a real bug of this kind. CVE-2026-21710 was a denial-of-service flaw in req.headersDistinct, and it went like this:

Because the exception is thrown synchronously inside a property getter, an 'error' event listener can’t catch it. The fix initialized the headersDistinct and trailersDistinct objects with { __proto__: null }, which is the behavior PR #62900 later extended to headers and trailers. The advisory covers headersDistinct only, so it doesn’t mean req.headers had the same crash. The bug also stopped at crashing the process: a header couldn’t use it to modify Object.prototype globally. And a null-prototype object removes inherited-property hazards only where the headers are created. If you merge headers into an ordinary object, that target still has the inherited __proto__ accessor.

Node.js 27 also updates its engine and bundled dependencies. Most of the V8 details below come from Joyee Cheung’s Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha) on the Node.js blog, which is worth reading in full if you maintain performance-sensitive code or native tooling:

Default Heap Limit up to 4 GB on mid-sized machines: When --max-old-space-size is not specified, V8 now sets the default old-generation heap limit to half of physical memory (or container cgroup memory), clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB. Previously, machines with less than 15 GB of RAM were capped at 2 GB. On an 8 GB container or VM, the default old-generation limit therefore rises from 2 GB to 4 GB (and on a 6 GB machine, from 2 GB to 3 GB). These are old-generation limits, not limits on the process’s total memory use.

Buffer and ArrayBuffer memory affects garbage collection scheduling: Memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances is now included in V8’s global allocation limit. If your app allocates large off-heap buffers (for example, image processing or large file buffers), this affects when garbage collection is scheduled. The global allocation limit is distinct from the old-generation heap limit and does not impose a hard cap on the process’s total memory.

Slightly more memory per worker and per native object: Each V8 isolate (the main thread and every worker thread) uses about 180 KB more for property lookup caches, and every JavaScript object that wraps a native resource (a socket, file handle, stream, hash, or blob) may use about 16 bytes more on the heap and about 50 bytes more outside it. That’s negligible for most apps, but it adds up if you spawn many workers or hold many open sockets.

Fewer hard crashes on fatal errors: More fatal V8 errors now go through Node.js’s fatal error handling before aborting, so --report-on-fatalerror can produce a diagnostic report in cases that previously aborted without one. Some extreme inputs (overly long template literals, classes with too many elements, a regexp too large to compile) now throw a RangeError instead of crashing the process. The V8 post is explicit that this isn’t guaranteed, so don’t build program logic around it.

These numbers come from V8’s own benchmarks, and the impact varies with platform, workload, and build configuration. Measure your application before counting on a speedup.

OpenSSL 4.1.0, Undici 8.12, SQLite 3.54, and npm 12.1.0: Node.js 27 upgrades its bundled cryptography to OpenSSL 4.1.0, strips out all legacy OpenSSL 1.x compatibility shims and engine APIs, bumps npm to 12.1.0, and updates NODE_MODULE_VERSION to 153.

The Alpha window gives you time to check for breaking changes before the stable release. Most applications won’t encounter all of these, but check your code and dependencies for the following changes.

As we saw in the HTTP section, the header dictionaries no longer have a prototype. Normal property access (req.headers['content-type']), destructuring, and Object.keys() work as before. What breaks is calling methods inherited from Object.prototype: req.headers.hasOwnProperty('authorization') now throws a TypeError (and calling a method looked up on a dictionary of external data was never a good idea anyway).

Replace it with Object.hasOwn(req.headers, 'authorization'), which doesn’t rely on the object’s prototype and works on both Node.js 26 and 27. Please don’t “fix” this by restoring Object.prototype on the headers object. The in operator still works on null-prototype objects, but the updated Node.js docs advise against using it here, and Object.hasOwn() expresses the own-property check you actually mean.

This runnable example shows both the failure and the fix. Keep in mind that checking for a header’s presence does not authenticate its value:

If you run multiple Node.js processes on a 6 GB or 8 GB machine and relied on the old implicit 2 GB heap cap to keep them from starving each other, pass --max-old-space-size=2048 explicitly. Similarly, if your application holds hundreds of megabytes of Buffer data in memory alongside a large JS heap, be aware that Buffer allocations now influence V8’s global allocation limit and garbage collection scheduling.

Most V8 changes are invisible, but a few can break code that depends on exact results:

The V8 changes post lists more edge cases, including fractional getTimezoneOffset() values for historical dates and stricter take()/drop() limits on iterators.

When testing your project or library against Node.js 27:

For production, the release date matters. For library authors and local experiments, there is already code to try:

If you want to install the Alpha side by side with your stable LTS runtime without messing up your system setup, check out our guide on 5 ways to install Node.js using version managers like fnm or nvm.

Want to write modern, production-ready Node.js?

Our book Node.js Design Patterns covers streams, iterators, async control flow, modules, and scalable architectures. The runtime changes each year; these patterns help you design applications across releases.

Node.js 27 starts the annual release schedule, with every major version going on to LTS. Its first Alpha includes V8 15.6, node:net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, fs.mkstemp(), and --allow-env.

I’d start by trying Iterator.zipKeyed() and Iterator.prototype.join() in a data-transformation script. They let you process parallel collections lazily without collecting intermediate arrays.

For the full list of commits and low-level details, check out the official Node.js 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 release notes and the companion post on Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha).

Thanks to the Node.js releasers, V8 maintainers, and contributors who worked on this first Alpha and the new release schedule.

Node.js 27 is the first version under the new Node.js release schedule. Instead of two major releases per year, Node.js now ships one major release every April, preceded by a six-month Alpha testing phase starting in October.

Yes. Under the new release schedule, the old odd/even rule is gone and every yearly major release becomes LTS. Node.js 27 will enter Current in April 2027, move to LTS in October 2027, and be supported until April 2030.

Thanks to V8 15.6, Node.js 27 ships Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), Math.sumPrecise(), and Intl.Locale.prototype.variants enabled by default.

When --max-old-space-size is not set, V8 now defaults to half of physical memory clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB (meaning an 8 GB machine gets a 4 GB heap instead of 2 GB). Additionally, memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances now counts toward V8’s global allocation limit, affecting when garbage collection runs.

If you are reading this before April 2027, keep production workloads on an LTS release. Node.js 27 is still in its Alpha testing phase during that period, intended for library authors, CI pipelines, and experimentation. It is scheduled to enter Current in April 2027 and LTS in October 2027. Once a stable release is available, evaluate it against your application’s support requirements.

#9905. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Android device manufacturer Videostrong allegedly ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

#9904. Critical security vulnerability affects OpenSSH on Alpine Linux systems

Version 10.6p2 of OpenSSH has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability that affects Linux systems that use musl libc with PAM disabled, such as Alpine Linux. OpenSSH developer Damien Miller said:

If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY.

This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication.

We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly.

The Alpine Linux project has announced that it will be backporting the OpenSSH fix "all the way back to Alpine 3.16", which was released in May 2022.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

#9903. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9902. Unattended reboots with encrypted disks

November 7, 2026 · About 7 minutes · Tags: blogsystem5, zkeys

This article was originally published on Substack in the Blog System/5 newsletter and is replicated here for archival purposes.

Do you run a small home server or NAS holding your precious photos and sensitive documents? If so, I suppose the drives are encrypted, right? But then… can you reboot the machine without manually entering a passphrase before being able to access your files again?

If you answered yes to the questions above—which is common for convenience—that implies the encryption keys live in the machine which… kinda defeats the purpose of disk encryption, doesn’t it? A thief can break into your house, lift the whole box (they are small these days, huh), plug it in elsewhere, and gain free rein over your files.

So, which one is it? Simplicity and reliability by allowing automatic reboots or data protection by keeping the key in your head? With ZKeys—a little new project I’m launching today—you can have your cake and eat it too.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

ZKeys is a managed service that stores encryption passphrases off-site. Client machines fetch the encryption keys from the service and keep those keys alive (unlocked) via periodic keepalive messages.

If the server stops receiving those messages for a long period of time (e.g. because it has been unplugged as part of theft), access to the key is automatically locked. You get automatic, passwordless reboots while keeping your data protected against real incidents.

About a year ago, I was reinstalling my FreeBSD home server to act as my NAS after a short stint with a Synology box. During that process, I decided to enable encryption for the ZFS data pool. But as I did that, I faced the question: how do I allow the machine to automatically serve my data after a reboot? I could put the key in a local file, which FreeBSD supports via the keylocation ZFS option, but that would render disk encryption pretty much useless.

So I had an idea: what if I put the key on a different machine away from my house? I could then make the NAS fetch the key to mount the drives. And if someone stole the server, I could wipe the remote key and make the data unreadable before they could plug it back in. I did post this to Twitter and there was some interest in the idea:

Silly or smart? I wrote a startup rc.d script to automatically mount my encrypted ZFS pool by fetching the key from a remote server. What I want to protect against is the "drives stolen from home" case. If that happened, I could quickly remove the key. https://t.co/eZle2nJlXW

But… did you notice the problem with what I said above? Wiping the key by hand after noticing something is wrong is problematic because the gap between those two events may be large. What if I’m on a long vacation and I have no means of noticing that the machine has been stolen? Game over.

So I refined the idea: what if I had a service that stored the key remotely and required the consuming machine to send it frequent pings to keep the key unlocked? This way, if the machine were stolen, it’d likely be offline for more than a few minutes and the service could automatically determine that something is wrong and lock the key from future accesses. And that’s precisely what ZKeys does.

Before getting into details, it’s important to get something out of the way early on: ZKeys is designed so that a compromise of the server is insufficient to retrieve or reconstruct your keys. This is done in two ways:

Split keys: The ZKeys server only stores half of the passphrase used to unlock a volume. The other half remains on the client machine. The zkeys client program combines both halves to produce the whole passphrase.

Encryption at rest: The keys are encrypted at rest with a password that the zkeys client must supply for retrieval and which is securely transmitted over HTTPS. The password only lives in the server’s memory for a brief period of time.

The tradeoff is, simply, that you MUST back up the full encryption keys in a third location of your own (a paper in a safe, a password manager, you name it). If ZKeys goes down or you lose your remote key password, there is absolutely nothing I can do to help you. You have been warned. The setup instructions later on will instruct you how to back the key up.

The ZKeys service is available at https://zkeys.jmmv.dev/ and the open-source client—along with system integrations for FreeBSD and Fedora—is in my jmmv/zkeys repository.

Disclaimer: ZKeys is offered to you for free. I make no promises about its reliability, availability, or anything else. I am giving you access because I expect that supporting a handful of extra users won’t be a big issue. But if support becomes a burden, or if load becomes unmanageable, I’ll have to re-evaluate my choices here. Which means that, for now, you have to use the limited LAUNCH50 code to get started!

The basic idea to set ZKeys up is the following:

That’s all it takes, but the steps are quite manual at the moment because no upstream OSes provide packages. The service documentation covers several scenarios in detail for FreeBSD and Fedora, so I’m not going to repeat them here.

Now for the nerdy details, because that’s what you’re here for:

The CLI is Rust, of course, but it has to come with a bunch of shell scripts to integrate with FreeBSD’s rc.d system and Fedora’s systemd and dracut. These integration points are the trickiest part of the client package and the hardest to validate automatically, which is why I only provide support for the two systems I use on a daily basis. It should be possible to integrate ZKeys with any other Unix-like OS, though.

The CLI package is a frankenmonster made up of Cargo and GNU Automake/Autoconf because of the above. I believe system-level tools should abide by de facto standard tooling even if such standard tooling is deficient, so GNU Autotools it is.

I run two non-replicated instances of the service: one in US West and one in EU West, because I have machines in both locations and both rely on encryption. I strongly suggest you use the US instance as I’m seeing frequent power hiccups in my EU deployment.

The frontend uses Bootstrap, straight from the 2010s. Does it look ugly? Maybe, but I kinda like it and, most importantly, it’s functional. Of course I could have asked AI to produce yet-another-dull-site full of gradients and slop, but I did not want to do that, so I stuck to what I already knew how to do by hand from previous services.

The admin page is an SPA, yes. This is an intentional design choice that forces a very clear separation between the backend APIs and the frontend. Whatever the current web frontend can do any other client can do as well. For example: the current zkeys CLI tool does not offer administrative operations but it could trivially be made to support them, because the APIs are right there.

The backend is built on my own III-IV framework which I’ve been building up over the last few years while implementing a couple of other services. I’ve had to add a lot more features to it to make this possible though.

Oops, I know that’s the name of a different effort, but you really need to encrypt your local drives. With computers becoming smaller and lighter every day, it’s easier than ever to steal them, and unfortunately home break-ins are common in some parts of the world. Block-level encryption is cheap in CPU terms, so do it. ZKeys just makes this process less cumbersome for headless servers.

Once again, head to https://zkeys.jmmv.dev/ to get started and use code LAUNCH50 to create an account!

And if you are interested in helping out, I’d appreciate the creation of packages for FreeBSD and Fedora, and integration scripts for other systems.

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL

Nov 07, 2026 3 min read

Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times.

According to the authors, pg_vectorsearch enables faster, more memory-efficient vector search directly in PostgreSQL, reducing the infrastructure required to handle large vector datasets. The extension supports existing pgvector columns, allowing applications to perform vector search without a separate database. To use the new capabilities, developers must install the extension and create a PRISM index on the vector column:

In Tiger Data’s own benchmarks using 100 million vectors, PRISM built an index in 1 hour and 40 minutes on a machine with 128 GB of memory, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) took 42 hours on a machine with 512 GB of memory. Formerly known as Timescale, Tiger Data is the company behind TimescaleDB, the open source PostgreSQL extension for time-series data and real-time analytics.

Erik Nordström, senior staff engineer at Tiger Data, Matvey Arye, principal engineer at Tiger Data, and Noah Hein, staff product marketing manager at Tiger Data, write:

PRISM brings a partition-based approach to PostgreSQL, similar to the approach used by newer dedicated vector search systems. Instead of connecting every vector to its neighbors in a graph, PRISM groups similar vectors into partitions and stores them as a list in a compressed format that is densely packed into database pages.

While HNSW is an approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm that quickly finds vectors similar to a query in large datasets, PRISM narrows searches to relevant partitions and scans compressed vectors sequentially. This reduces index size and avoids costly random memory or disk access, enabling faster vector search with less RAM directly in PostgreSQL.

Michael Freedman, cofounder and CTO of Tiger Data, published an article describing the architecture of the PRISM vector index. The index in pg_vectorsearch combines hierarchical clustering to narrow the search space, compressed vectors for efficient sequential scanning, and RaBitQ quantization to reduce expensive distance calculations. It duplicates vectors near partition boundaries to improve recall and relies on PostgreSQL’s native storage, logging, and concurrency mechanisms.

Incremental rebalancing is not yet fully implemented, so frequent data changes may require rebuilding the index to maintain search efficiency. Freedman explains:

The harder problem is maintaining the clustering as the dataset changes. Centroids don't automatically move when new vectors arrive, and posting lists gradually lose their original physical locality. We currently support limited on-demand splitting of oversized posting lists for flat indexes, but the more general rebalancing operations, including merging and reassignment, are not implemented yet.

In a popular Hacker News thread, the overall reaction is one of technical interest but caution. Practitioners see potential in faster vector search with lower memory requirements inside PostgreSQL, but raise questions about independent benchmark validation, whether pg_vectorsearch could replace pgvectorscale, and the lack of support for filtered searches. Hermon Hagos comments:

Vector search just got cheaper (...) For those of us building RAG apps on one database and a tight budget, that matters. Fast semantic search without spinning up a separate vector store or a bigger server is real money saved. It is still alpha, so do not ship it to clients yet, but this is one to watch closely.

Although not independently validated, Tiger Data’s benchmarks use an open source tool, measure recall@10 against exact search results, and compare both indexes under the same PostgreSQL configuration and instance types, using pgvector’s 16-bit halfvec for HNSW.

The new vector extension requires PostgreSQL 18 or later and currently supports vectors with up to 1968 dimensions. Filtered vector searches combining WHERE and ORDER BY are not supported until general availability. The project's code is available on GitHub. Tiger Data plans to move its existing pgvectorscale extension into maintenance mode.

#9899. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.
